title: Great Teaching Is Neither Scripted nor Improvised
author: Nathaniel Swain
summary: Swain argues that expert teaching lives between two extremes: rigid script-following and reactive improvisation. Using a two-by-two matrix, he defines four teaching modes—responsive, reactive, rigid, and derivative—where only responsive teaching (well-prepared and willing to deviate purposefully) represents genuine expertise. Meaningful preparation is what makes meaningful deviation possible; it encompasses knowing content, knowing students, and knowing how learning happens, not just assembling a slide deck. When preparation is shallow, even student questions feel threatening rather than revealing. In well-calibrated schools, shared planning and high-quality curriculum materials reduce unnecessary variation and free teachers to refine rather than recreate from scratch. Structure is the foundation of professional judgment, not its enemy. The best teachers give students the lesson they need, not just the lesson they have planned.
points: Expert teaching occupies the 'responsive' quadrant: well-prepared AND willing to deviate purposefully—as opposed to reactive (improvising without preparation), rigid (prepared but inflexible), or derivative (dependent on someone else's script).

Meaningful preparation goes beyond a slide deck: it means knowing content deeply, anticipating misconceptions, recognizing cognitive overload, and understanding when to explain, model, question, practise, or extend.
Deviation has Latin roots in 'via' (road/way)—leaving the path only has value if you know where you're going and how to return; aimless deviation is wandering, not teaching.
In well-calibrated schools, shared planning reduces unnecessary variation so teachers spend time refining and augmenting materials rather than recreating everything from scratch.
Structure is not a straitjacket—it is the foundation that allows professional judgment to flourish, and the goal is always to give students the lesson they need, not just the lesson planned.
quotes: At one end is rigid delivery : faithfully following a script regardless of what students understand, misunderstand, or need. At the other is reactive improvisation : making teaching decisions on the fly without a secure plan or deep knowledge to guide them.
Meaningful preparation is what makes meaningful deviation possible.
A teacher who refuses to deviate is trapped by the lesson plan. A teacher who constantly deviates without purpose is simply wandering.
Structure is not a straitjacket. It is the foundation that allows professional judgement to flourish.
The best teachers are those that are prepared enough to know exactly when, why, and how to depart from a well-structured plan in service of student learning and curiosity.

When teachers do not understand the underlying concepts within the curriculum, the common misconceptions students are likely to experience, or the signs that cognitive overload is occurring, deviations become frightening.
